title: Design a Scalable Enterprise Frontend
description: Senior/lead system-design scenario covering domain boundaries, team ownership, dependency direction, lazy delivery, shared infrastructure and long-term maintainability.

blocks.title: Architect-level framing
blocks.content:
I would begin with business capabilities and ownership, not with folders named components, services and utils. I would identify stable domains such as identity, customer servicing, payments, reporting and administration, then give every domain a clear public API and an owning team. Inside each domain I would separate presentation, feature orchestration, data access and domain models so UI components do not call arbitrary endpoints or import another feature's internals.

I would normally start with a modular monolith. Major routes would be lazy loaded, and dependency rules would permit feature code to depend on platform and design-system libraries, but not on another feature's private implementation. Cross-domain communication would happen through explicit navigation, typed contracts or a small application-level orchestration layer. I would keep authentication, configuration, telemetry, error normalization and the design system shared; I would not put business rules or a universal global store into a shared folder.

The API boundary matters as much as the component tree. I would generate or validate typed clients from an OpenAPI contract, use a BFF only where aggregation, token isolation or frontend-specific payloads justify it, and make API compatibility part of release planning. For state, I would keep local UI state in the component, share feature workflow state only within the feature, represent shareable filters in the URL and treat server data as cacheable remote state.

Finally, I would make the architecture executable. CI would enforce dependency boundaries, code ownership, bundle budgets, contract checks, accessibility checks and test gates. Architecture decisions would include assumptions and reversal criteria. I would validate the design using lead time, cross-team change frequency, bundle growth, route performance, production error ownership and how often one feature change forces unrelated teams to coordinate. If independent deployment later becomes a proven bottleneck, I would evaluate micro-frontends; I would not start there only because the organization has many teams.
keyPoints: Organize by business capability and ownership; expose explicit feature APIs and prohibit deep imports.
Prefer a modular monolith first. Add micro-frontends only for demonstrated independent-deployment or organizational needs.
Keep platform concerns shared, but keep feature rules, feature state and API orchestration owned by the feature.

title: Domain Boundaries and Dependency Rules
description: How to divide a large frontend into business domains, prevent circular dependencies and make module boundaries enforceable.

blocks.title: Architect-level framing
blocks.content:
I would first map the current dependency graph and change history instead of immediately moving files. Circular imports are usually a symptom that ownership and direction are unclear. I would group code by business capability, identify shared vocabulary that truly belongs to a stable domain model, and distinguish reusable UI primitives from business-specific components that merely look similar.

Each domain would expose a small public entry point. Consumers could import contracts, route configuration or a deliberately shared facade, but not internal components, reducers or HTTP services. I would define a dependency direction such as application shell -> feature -> data access/domain -> platform/design system. A lower layer must never import a higher layer, and peer features should not call one another's private services. If two domains need coordination, the application layer can orchestrate them or the backend can expose a workflow API.

I would migrate incrementally. First I would prevent new violations with lint or workspace constraints. Then I would break cycles around high-change areas, replace deep imports with public APIs, move duplicated primitive UI into the design system, and move shared business logic to the domain that owns the rule. I would avoid a large 'common' package because it recreates the same problem under a different name.

At lead level I would also define ownership. Every public contract needs an owner, compatibility policy and deprecation path. The success criteria are not just zero circular imports: feature teams should be able to change internal implementation without forcing consumers to update, and dependency violations should fail in CI before they reach code review.
keyPoints: Use business ownership and change patterns to define domains, not only technical file types.
Expose small public APIs and block deep imports into feature internals.
Define a one-way dependency graph and use an application orchestration layer for cross-domain workflows.
Stop new violations first, then migrate high-risk cycles incrementally.
Do not turn a shared/common library into a dumping ground for business logic.
Assign owners and compatibility rules to every cross-domain contract.

title: API Contracts and Backward Compatibility
description: Designing typed frontend/backend contracts, compatible evolution, deprecation, validation and mixed-version deployments.

blocks.title: Architect-level framing
blocks.content:
I would treat the API contract as a product with consumers, not as an implementation detail of the current backend. First I would identify the compatibility window: how long old browser tabs, cached assets, mobile releases and partner clients can remain active. Then I would prefer additive evolution—new optional fields, new endpoints or new enum values—over renaming or changing meaning in place.

The contract would be described in OpenAPI or another machine-readable schema and reviewed together with examples and error behavior. Frontend types can be generated, but generated TypeScript is not runtime validation; at trust boundaries I would still validate critical payloads or fail safely when the response shape is invalid. Consumer-driven contract tests and compatibility checks should run in CI before either side deploys.

For a breaking change I would use a migration sequence: backend supports old and new forms, clients migrate and emit version/usage telemetry, the old form is deprecated with an owner and date, and only then is it removed. I would avoid using a URL version for every small additive change, but a new major endpoint or media type is reasonable when semantics fundamentally change.

I would also standardize errors. A predictable problem-details shape with a machine-readable code lets the UI map validation, authorization and retryable failures without parsing human text. Unknown fields should be ignored where safe, and the client should handle unknown enum values with a fallback rather than crashing.

The design is successful when frontend and backend can deploy independently during the agreed window, rollback remains possible, and telemetry shows when deprecated contracts are no longer used.

title: Choosing REST, GraphQL or a BFF
description: Selecting an API interaction model based on data ownership, aggregation, caching, security, client diversity and operational cost.

blocks.title: Architect-level framing
blocks.content:
I would not select a technology from the number of endpoints alone. I would first clarify who owns the client experience, whether multiple client types need different shapes, how frequently the composition changes, whether browser credentials may call downstream services directly, and what latency and caching requirements exist.

Direct REST calls are appropriate when the APIs already expose client-friendly resources, request count is manageable and the browser is allowed to access them. The browser can parallelize independent requests, and HTTP semantics and CDN caching remain straightforward. The downside is chattiness, duplicated orchestration and exposure of backend topology.

A BFF is attractive here because security wants server-side token handling and the dashboard has a frontend-specific aggregate. The BFF can own the session, call downstream services, apply timeouts, normalize errors and return a view model. It must remain a composition/security boundary rather than duplicating core business rules. I would isolate downstream failures so one optional widget does not fail the whole response.

GraphQL becomes compelling when many clients need flexible, evolving projections over a connected domain and the organization can operate schema governance, authorization, query-cost controls, caching and observability. It is not automatically faster; a poorly designed resolver graph can move N+1 and over-fetching problems to the server.

For this scenario I would likely choose an Angular -> BFF -> services design, potentially with GraphQL behind or at the BFF only if the domain and client diversity justify it. I would validate with end-to-end latency, number of downstream calls, payload size, partial-failure behavior, cacheability, authorization correctness and operational ownership.
keyPoints: Choose from client diversity, aggregation needs, security boundaries, caching and organizational capability—not fashion.
Direct REST is simple when resources are client-friendly and browser access is acceptable.
A BFF can isolate tokens, aggregate services and return frontend-specific view models.
GraphQL requires schema governance, field authorization, query-cost limits and resolver observability.
Keep authoritative business rules in domain services, not in the BFF.
Design partial failure and timeouts explicitly for aggregated responses.

title: Multi-Tenant Frontend Architecture
description: Designing tenant isolation, branding, runtime configuration, permissions, caching and observability for a SaaS frontend.

blocks.title: Architect-level framing
blocks.content:
I would separate tenant customization from tenant security. Branding, navigation and feature presentation can be driven by a validated runtime tenant configuration, but the browser must never be the authority for tenant isolation or entitlements. Every API request and data access must be scoped and authorized by the backend using the authenticated tenant context.

At bootstrap, the application can resolve the tenant from an approved hostname or server session, then load a signed or trusted configuration containing public values such as design tokens, enabled modules, locale defaults and support links. I would validate the schema, apply safe defaults and cache it by tenant plus version. I would not place secrets, database identifiers or authorization decisions in that file.

The UI should ask capability questions such as `can('payment.approve')` rather than compare tenant names or hard-coded roles. Tenant-specific components should be exceptional; most variation should be configuration, content and design tokens so the codebase remains testable. Where regulation requires data residency, the region routing decision belongs at the edge/BFF/backend, not in an editable browser setting.

Caching and telemetry need tenant awareness without leaking sensitive identifiers. Private responses must not enter a shared CDN cache, and cache keys must include all relevant variation such as tenant and locale. Logs and metrics can use a pseudonymous tenant key, while PII is redacted.

I would test horizontal isolation aggressively: manipulate tenant IDs, URLs, cached data and multi-tab sessions. I would also test configuration combinations to avoid an exponential matrix, using supported tenant profiles and contract validation. The architecture is correct only when changing browser state cannot expose another tenant's data.
keyPoints: Treat tenant configuration as presentation input, never as the authorization boundary.
Resolve tenant from a trusted server/session context and enforce tenant scope on every API operation.
Drive most variation through validated runtime config and design tokens, not forks per customer.
Centralize capability checks and avoid hard-coded tenant or role comparisons.
Partition private caches and telemetry to prevent cross-tenant leakage.
Test hostile tenant-ID manipulation, stale caches and cross-tab account switching.

title: Architecture Decisions and Fitness Functions
description: Making architectural choices explicit, measurable and continuously enforceable instead of relying on slide decks.

blocks.title: Architect-level framing
blocks.content:
I would convert the architecture from advice into executable constraints. First I would record important decisions in short Architecture Decision Records: context, decision, alternatives, consequences, owner, date and conditions that would cause us to revisit it. The ADR is useful for understanding why, but it does not enforce anything.

For each critical property I would define a fitness function—a repeatable check that tells us whether the architecture still has that property. Dependency rules can be enforced with workspace tags or lint rules; circular imports and deep imports can fail CI; initial and route bundle budgets can be checked from build statistics; OpenAPI compatibility can be checked against the previous contract; design-system and accessibility standards can run component tests; critical user journeys can have performance and availability SLOs.

I would avoid hundreds of blocking rules on day one. Start with the few risks that are expensive to reverse: domain coupling, public API compatibility, security headers, bundle growth and unsupported browser targets. Existing debt can be baselined so the rule prevents regression while teams migrate incrementally. Every exception should be time-bounded, owned and visible.

Architecture review then becomes evidence-based. A dashboard can show trends for bundle size, dependency violations, duplicated libraries, API compatibility and test reliability. When a rule becomes counterproductive, update the ADR and fitness function rather than encouraging teams to bypass it.

The senior answer is not 'write more documentation'. It is to connect architectural intent to CI, observability and ownership so violations are discovered at the cheapest possible point.
keyPoints: Use ADRs to preserve context and reversal criteria; use automated fitness functions to enforce properties.
Automate dependency boundaries, bundle budgets, contract compatibility, security and quality gates.

Make exceptions explicit, owned and expiring.

Change the rule deliberately when constraints change; do not normalize silent bypasses.

title: Build vs Buy and Third-Party Dependencies
description: Evaluating libraries and SaaS widgets using product fit, accessibility, security, performance, maintenance and exit strategy.

blocks.title: Architect-level framing
blocks.content:
I would begin with capabilities and risk, not a feature checklist from vendor demos. For each component I would classify what is commodity and what is a differentiating business workflow. A data grid with virtualization, keyboard navigation, pinned columns and export is expensive to build correctly; adopting a maintained library may be sensible. A simple company-specific status card is usually cheaper to own than to force through a generic framework.

The evaluation would include accessibility behavior, performance with our worst-case data, framework and browser compatibility, security history, release cadence, maintainer health, licensing, bundle impact, SSR support, theming, localization, testability and whether the API allows us to wrap it behind our own abstraction. For a paid product I would also examine support SLA, data processing, hosting location, lock-in, upgrade policy and contract exit terms.

I would run a time-boxed proof of concept using real requirements—not a toy page. The POC should include 100,000-row virtualization, keyboard-only operation, screen-reader behavior, custom cell rendering, dark/RTL themes, error states and production build analysis. Security should review third-party scripts and any data sent to vendor infrastructure.

I would isolate the decision. Product code should depend on an internal adapter or design-system component where practical, not on vendor APIs in hundreds of screens. That gives us a migration seam, but I would not build an abstraction so generic that it exposes every vendor feature and becomes harder than the dependency itself.

The final decision should document total cost of ownership and an exit plan. 'Free' open source still has integration, upgrade and incident cost; building gives control but creates permanent maintenance responsibility.

title: Frontend Platform and Golden Path
description: Creating a paved road for teams: templates, CI, observability, security, design system, ownership and controlled extensibility.

blocks.title: Architect-level framing
blocks.content:
I would build a paved road, not a centralized team that approves every component. The platform should provide a supported application and feature template with secure defaults: bootstrap configuration, identity integration, HTTP client policies, normalized errors, telemetry, design-system setup, testing utilities, lint rules, bundle budgets and deployment pipeline. Teams should get these capabilities by default rather than copying wiki snippets.

The platform contract must be small and versioned. I would separate stable primitives from product-specific orchestration, publish migration guides and automate upgrades where possible. A platform package that owns every business decision will become a bottleneck, so feature teams retain domain state, workflows and release accountability.

title: Caching Strategy Across Browser, CDN and Client State
description: Layered caching for static assets, API responses and client query state with explicit freshness, privacy and invalidation rules.

blocks.title: Architect-level framing
blocks.content:
I would separate cacheable resources by ownership, sensitivity and acceptable staleness. Static build assets are the easiest case: JavaScript, CSS, fonts and images should use content-hashed filenames and long-lived immutable caching. The application shell or `index.html` should revalidate so it can discover the newest asset hashes. That avoids the common failure where an old shell points at chunks that no longer exist.

For API data I would start with HTTP semantics before inventing a JavaScript cache. Public reference data such as country codes can use `Cache-Control`, validators such as `ETag`, and possibly a CDN. Private customer data must use appropriate `private`/`no-store` or short-lived policies and must never be stored in a shared cache. `Vary` and cache keys must include the dimensions that actually change the response, such as locale or representation.

Inside Angular I would use a bounded server-state cache to deduplicate requests and provide a deliberate stale-while-revalidate experience where the business allows it. Every entry needs a key, freshness duration, invalidation rule, privacy classification and memory limit. Balances may be fetched on entry and after mutations or focus regain; mostly-static product metadata can remain fresh much longer.

I would not cache error responses blindly, and I would distinguish 'stale but usable' from 'unknown'. After a write, update the canonical entity and invalidate dependent summaries rather than clearing the whole application. Offline storage is a separate decision because persisted data has security, quota and migration implications.

I would validate the design using transfer bytes, conditional-request rate, CDN/browser hit ratio, stale-data incidents, memory growth and behavior during deployment and account switching.

Prefer HTTP caching and validators before adding custom client caches.

title: Cache Invalidation and Stale Data
description: Maintaining consistent entity and derived-query caches after writes, external changes, reconnects and optimistic updates.

blocks.title: Architect-level framing
blocks.content:
I would first define a canonical identity and ownership model. If three components each keep a long-lived copy of the same vehicle, invalidation becomes guesswork. I would represent the entity by a stable ID in one feature-level server-state cache or normalized store, while lists and dashboards keep query membership and derive the latest entity fields from that canonical record.

After the mutation succeeds, I would update the returned canonical entity and invalidate or patch every dependent query whose membership or aggregation might have changed. Renaming may only require updating the entity for lists that reference it; changing status may also invalidate dashboard counts. The mutation contract should return the authoritative updated representation and version, not force the client to reconstruct business rules.

For optimistic UI, I would capture the previous state, apply the temporary change, disable or sequence conflicting writes, and roll back or reconcile if the server rejects it. When concurrent editors matter, I would use an ETag/version with `If-Match` so the server can reject lost updates. For changes made by other users, freshness can be maintained through focus/reconnect revalidation, short TTLs, polling or versioned real-time events depending on the requirement.

I would make staleness visible where it matters. A trading balance and a vehicle display name do not deserve the same policy. The UI should know whether it is showing confirmed, pending or stale data.

Validation would include mutation followed by navigation, multiple tabs, offline/reconnect, rejected optimistic writes, out-of-order responses and cross-user updates. The goal is not 'never cache'; it is to make the consistency model explicit.

title: Performance Investigation for a Large Dashboard
description: An evidence-led workflow for separating network, JavaScript, Angular rendering, DOM, layout, paint and third-party costs.

blocks.title: Architect-level framing
blocks.content:
I would not begin by adding `OnPush` everywhere. I would create a repeatable profile on representative hardware and network conditions, then divide the delay into phases: document and asset transfer, JavaScript parse/execute, authentication/config bootstrap, API waterfall, Angular render work, DOM/layout/paint and long tasks from charts or transformations.

The browser network panel and performance trace show whether requests are sequential, duplicated or blocked by a large initial bundle. Angular DevTools or the Angular track in Chrome can identify components with repeated change detection, expensive lifecycle hooks and template computations. A bundle analyzer reveals duplicated libraries and heavy code loaded before it is needed. Real-user monitoring tells me whether the lab reproduces actual browser/device segments.

Then I would classify widgets. Critical above-the-fold widgets load first; independent requests run in parallel with per-widget error states; heavy charts, PDF engines and editors are lazy or `@defer` loaded; below-the-fold widgets load on viewport or interaction; large lists are virtualized; stale requests are cancelled; expensive transformations move out of templates and possibly into a worker. I would reserve layout space for deferred content to avoid CLS.

I would also challenge the API shape. Thirty widgets should not automatically mean thirty uncontrolled calls. A BFF or batched endpoint may help where network round trips dominate, but one giant endpoint can create head-of-line blocking and all-or-nothing failure. The right grouping follows criticality and ownership.

Each change must be remeasured against a budget: first useful content, interaction latency, long-task time, bytes, API p95, DOM size and error rate. I would ship incrementally and compare field metrics by build so we know which change helped.

title: Bundle Size and Code Splitting
description: Reducing initial JavaScript without creating route waterfalls, duplicated dependencies or unusable deferred interactions.

blocks.title: Architect-level framing
blocks.content:
I would inspect the production build graph first. Raw source size is not enough; I want compressed transfer, parse/compile/execute time and which routes actually need each dependency. A bundle analyzer can identify duplicated packages, barrel imports that pull in unrelated exports, eager route references and libraries with poor tree-shaking.

The first boundary is usually navigation. Standalone route components or feature routes should use `loadComponent`/`loadChildren` so users do not download administration, reports and settings on the landing screen. Within a route, Angular `@defer` is useful for heavy standalone widgets. PDF generation, rich-text editing, mapping and complex charts are strong candidates for dynamic import when the user opens that feature.

I would remove unused and duplicate dependencies before replacing libraries. If a 500 KB library supplies one utility, a native API or smaller focused package may be appropriate, but migration risk and correctness matter. I would also verify that the same framework/runtime dependency is not bundled into multiple micro-frontends.

Code splitting is not free. Too many tiny chunks can create request and execution overhead, while prefetching everything defeats the purpose. I would prefetch high-probability next routes during idle or after intent, and test on realistic network latency. Deferred placeholders must preserve layout and accessibility.

Finally, I would add CI budgets for initial and critical route chunks, with an allowlist process for deliberate growth. Success is lower time to usable—not simply more chunk files.

title: Large Lists and Data Grids
description: Server-side query design, virtualization, stable selection, aggregation, export and accessibility for very large datasets.

blocks.title: Architect-level framing

title: Main-Thread CPU, Long Tasks and Web Workers
description: Keeping interactions responsive when parsing, transforming, compressing or calculating large datasets.

blocks.title: Architect-level framing
blocks.content:
I would first profile the task to confirm CPU is the bottleneck and identify the exact operations. A worker does not make inefficient algorithms free; it moves suitable computation off the UI thread. I would reduce input size, avoid repeated transformations, choose an appropriate algorithm and only then decide whether the remaining work should run in a Web Worker or on the backend.

A dedicated worker is useful for pure CPU-heavy tasks such as parsing large files, aggregation, compression or complex calculations that do not need DOM access. I would define a typed message protocol with request IDs, progress, cancellation and error responses. Data passed to workers is structured-cloned by default, so very large copies can become expensive; transferable `ArrayBuffer` objects or chunked streaming can reduce copying where appropriate.

The main thread owns UI state and DOM rendering. It sends a bounded job to the worker, displays progress, keeps controls responsive and ignores late results from cancelled jobs. The worker should be lazily loaded because many users may never run the report. For calculations that must be authoritative, security-sensitive or too large for browser memory, I would use an asynchronous backend job instead.

I would verify the result numerically and operationally: main-thread long tasks, INP, worker startup, total completion time, memory on both sides, cancellation, browser support and behavior when the tab is backgrounded. A faster total calculation that still blocks the UI is not acceptable; equally, a responsive UI with doubled total time may not meet the workflow SLA.

title: Large File Upload, Download and Streaming
description: Designing resumable transfers, progress, integrity, memory safety and asynchronous server processing.

blocks.title: Architect-level framing
blocks.content:
I would separate transfer from processing. For uploads, the browser first creates an upload session with metadata, allowed file type, size and authorization. The file is sent in bounded chunks with a stable upload ID, part numbers or byte ranges and integrity checks. Completed parts can be retried without restarting the whole file, and the server finalizes only when every part is present and valid. The UI persists only safe resume metadata, displays confirmed server progress and supports cancellation.

The browser must not read the entire file into memory. I would slice the `File` object into chunks and limit concurrency to avoid saturating memory and network. Virus scanning, schema validation and business processing happen on the server after upload, usually as an asynchronous job. The upload endpoint stores data outside the web root and never trusts file name, MIME type or client validation alone.

For downloads, the best option is usually a server-generated object with a short-lived authorized URL and support for HTTP range/resume. If the application must transform a response client-side, use streams and write incrementally where supported rather than collecting a giant Blob. Browser support and enterprise policy may require a simpler server download path.

I would define idempotency and expiry for upload sessions, protect against duplicate finalization, enforce quotas and clean abandoned parts. Progress is based on acknowledged bytes, not merely bytes handed to the browser network stack.

Validation covers network interruption, tab close/reopen, duplicate chunks, out-of-order completion, checksum failure, quota exhaustion, malicious files and authorization expiry.

title: Memory Leaks and Long-Running Sessions
description: Finding retained components, subscriptions, DOM nodes, caches, event listeners and third-party resources in enterprise SPAs.

blocks.title: Architect-level framing
blocks.content:
I would create a deterministic reproduction: navigate through the same routes, open and close dialogs, refresh data and repeat the cycle while recording heap and DOM counters. A single high heap value is not enough; I need to see whether memory returns after garbage collection and which objects remain retained.

Heap snapshots and allocation timelines can show detached DOM nodes, component instances, chart objects, timers, event listeners and cached responses that remain reachable. Common Angular causes include manual subscriptions that outlive a component, global services retaining component callbacks, unbounded `shareReplay` or Maps, repeated event registration and third-party widgets not being destroyed. Modern Angular helpers such as `takeUntilDestroyed` reduce subscription lifecycle mistakes, but they do not solve unbounded caches or external resources automatically.

I would fix the ownership boundary, not merely call `unsubscribe` everywhere. The object that creates a timer, observer, worker, chart or listener owns its cleanup. Feature-scoped state should not accidentally become root-scoped. Caches need TTL/size eviction and must clear on logout or tenant switch. WebSocket and polling streams should have one managed connection rather than one per component render.

After each fix I would rerun the exact navigation loop, compare retained object counts and use field telemetry for long sessions where available. I would also add regression tests for high-risk components, although browser memory tests can be noisy.

title: Edge/CDN Delivery and Network Resilience
description: Static delivery, cache keys, compression, origin shielding, timeouts, retries and graceful behavior on slow or unstable networks.

blocks.title: Architect-level framing
blocks.content:
I would split static delivery from dynamic data. Content-hashed frontend assets are excellent CDN candidates: compress with Brotli/gzip, cache immutably at the edge and keep previous versions during a deployment grace period. The app shell revalidates and should be small. Public, identical reference data may also be cached at the edge with correct validators and cache keys.

Private user responses require much more caution. I would normally avoid shared CDN caching unless the platform has a proven private-cache design. `Authorization`, cookies, tenant, locale and query parameters affect whether responses can be shared; a missing variation dimension can become a data breach. The origin or BFF remains authoritative for identity and authorization.

For APIs, I would reduce latency through regional routing or a BFF close to users only when data residency and service topology allow it. Client retries are bounded, use backoff/jitter and apply only to safe/idempotent operations. A timeout should leave a useful localized error or cached read-only fallback when the business allows it. The UI should detect offline state as a hint, not a guarantee, and recover on reconnect.

I would use telemetry to separate DNS/TLS/connect time, TTFB, transfer and server time by region. Synthetic tests help availability, while RUM shows actual user networks. Changes such as edge caching or compression must be validated against cache correctness, privacy headers and rollback behavior.

The architecture is not 'put everything behind a CDN'. It is to place reusable bytes close to users while preserving security, freshness and observability.

title: Authentication with OIDC/OAuth for Browser Applications
description: Choosing OIDC/OAuth flows and SPA/BFF architectures while protecting redirects, tokens, sessions and logout.

blocks.title: Architect-level framing
blocks.content:
I would not implement username/password handling in Angular. The application should delegate authentication to the organization's OpenID Connect provider and use a maintained, standards-compliant client or a server-side BFF/session architecture.

The first decision is the browser architecture. For a pure SPA, the supported flow is Authorization Code with PKCE. The browser is a public client, so it must not contain a client secret. Redirect URIs must be exact and allowlisted; `state`, PKCE and, for OIDC, `nonce` are transaction-bound and validated. Access tokens should be short-lived, narrowly scoped and renewed through the provider-supported mechanism.

For a high-value banking application, I would strongly consider a BFF. The BFF performs the authorization-code exchange, keeps OAuth tokens server-side and gives the browser a Secure, HttpOnly, appropriately SameSite session cookie. The browser calls only the BFF, which applies CSRF defenses and forwards authorized requests. This reduces token theft through JavaScript but does not remove XSS risk—malicious code may still act as the user—so content security remains critical.

Authentication and authorization are separate. Login establishes identity; every API operation must authorize the subject, tenant, resource and action. I would define session inactivity and absolute timeouts, step-up authentication for sensitive operations, coordinated logout, revocation behavior and safe handling of expired sessions across tabs.

I would threat-model redirect manipulation, login CSRF, token replay, malicious third-party scripts and compromised tabs. Telemetry should capture flow failures without logging codes or tokens. The design must follow the identity provider's supported guidance rather than custom token parsing or home-grown refresh logic.

title: Token and Session Storage
description: Evaluating memory, Web Storage and HttpOnly cookie designs based on XSS, CSRF, persistence, multi-tab behavior and operational constraints.

blocks.title: Architect-level framing
blocks.content:
I would answer that storage is an architecture decision, not a one-line rule. Any token readable by JavaScript is exposed to malicious JavaScript running in the same origin. `localStorage`, `sessionStorage` and IndexedDB differ in persistence and APIs, but none protects a bearer token from XSS. Putting tokens in memory reduces persistence and cross-tab exposure, but a page refresh loses them and the running page can still read them.

For sensitive enterprise applications, my preferred design is often a BFF or server session. OAuth tokens remain server-side; the browser receives a Secure, HttpOnly cookie with a restrictive SameSite policy. JavaScript cannot read the cookie, which reduces direct token theft. Because the browser attaches cookies automatically, state-changing requests need an appropriate CSRF design and the backend must validate origin/session intent.

If a pure SPA must hold an access token, I would follow the identity provider and current browser-application OAuth guidance: Authorization Code with PKCE, short-lived and least-privileged access, no client secret, minimal persistence, no logging, and strong XSS prevention. I would avoid long-lived refresh tokens unless the provider has a supported rotation and replay-detection design for public clients.

Session lifecycle also matters: idle and absolute timeouts, logout/revocation, multi-tab synchronization, tenant/account switching and clearing cached user data. I would never put tokens in URLs because they leak through history, logs and referrers.

The correct interview answer explicitly connects token placement to threat model and states that frontend route guards or hidden buttons do not secure resources; server-side authorization remains authoritative.

title: Authorization: RBAC, Permissions and ABAC
description: Designing capability-based UI behavior while keeping resource authorization authoritative on the server.

blocks.title: Architect-level framing
blocks.content:
I would separate the frontend user experience from the security decision. The frontend needs enough information to hide or disable unavailable actions and explain why, but the backend must authorize every operation because browser state and requests can be modified.

I would avoid scattering checks such as `user.role === 'admin'` through templates. Instead, the application asks capability questions—`can('payment.approve', context)`—through a policy facade. Roles can be one input, but the returned permission model may include explicit capabilities and relevant constraints. For context-dependent rules such as region, ownership or amount, the server should evaluate the authoritative resource state. The UI can perform a preliminary check for usability, then handle a server denial correctly if state changed.

For list screens, I would not download unauthorized records and merely hide them. APIs filter data by subject and tenant. For individual actions, server policy uses subject, resource, action and environmental attributes. Highly sensitive operations can require step-up authentication, maker-checker separation and audit records.

Permission data has a lifecycle. It should be refreshed after login, role changes or tenant switching, and a server denial should not be treated as an impossible client bug. Feature flags and permissions are different: a flag controls rollout; a permission controls who may perform an action. Neither should contain secrets in browser code.

I would test vertical and horizontal privilege escalation, direct API calls, stale permissions, object ID manipulation and combinations of roles/attributes. The architecture should use least privilege and deny safely when policy data is missing.

title: XSS, CSP and Trusted Types
description: Preventing injection through safe rendering, contextual handling, sanitization and browser-enforced defense in depth.

blocks.title: Architect-level framing
blocks.content:
I would first reduce the problem. Plain user text should render through normal Angular interpolation or text properties, where the framework applies contextual escaping. Rich content should use a constrained document format—such as a limited Markdown or structured editor model—rather than accepting arbitrary HTML when the business does not require it.

If HTML is unavoidable, I would define a reviewed trust boundary. The content is sanitized with an allowlist designed for the required tags, attributes and URL schemes. Sanitization may happen server-side for stored content and again or through Angular's supported sanitization path at render time, because storage and rendering contexts can change. I would never solve the problem by broadly calling `bypassSecurityTrustHtml`; that marks content trusted without making it safe.

I would inventory dangerous sinks: `innerHTML`, `outerHTML`, `document.write`, dynamic script URLs, event-handler attributes and unsafe URL construction. Direct DOM manipulation should go through reviewed abstractions. Content Security Policy should be deployed as defense in depth, preferably starting in report-only mode and moving toward a strict nonce/hash policy. Trusted Types can force dangerous DOM sinks through approved policies in supporting browsers.

Third-party scripts are part of the XSS threat model because they execute with page privileges. I would minimize them, load only where needed, use CSP/SRI or sandboxing where applicable and ensure sensitive data is not exposed in the DOM.

Testing includes stored/reflected/DOM payloads, encoded variants, URL schemes, SVG/MathML cases, CSP reports and regression tests for the sanitizer policy. CSP is not a replacement for safe output handling; it is a second layer.

title: CSRF, CORS and SameSite
description: Understanding origin policy, cookie-based request forgery and layered server/client defenses.

blocks.title: Architect-level framing
blocks.content:
No. I would explain each control separately. CORS controls whether browser JavaScript from another origin can read or make certain credentialed cross-origin requests; it is not authentication and it does not stop non-browser clients. CSRF is possible when a browser automatically attaches credentials, such as cookies, to an attacker-triggered state-changing request.

`SameSite` is useful defense in depth, but the correct value depends on legitimate cross-site login and navigation flows, browser coverage and whether untrusted sibling subdomains are considered same-site. It should not be the only control for high-impact operations. The backend should use a framework-supported CSRF mechanism, such as a synchronizer token or signed double-submit/cookie-to-header pattern, and validate `Origin`/Fetch Metadata where appropriate. State-changing operations must not use GET.

For Angular with a same-origin BFF, the server can issue an XSRF token cookie readable by the application, and Angular's HTTP client can echo it in a custom header. The session cookie remains HttpOnly. An attacker site can cause the browser to send a cookie, but cannot normally read the token and set the approved custom header because of same-origin/CORS restrictions. The server validates both.

Credentialed CORS must allow only exact trusted origins, never `*`, and should not use loose regular expressions over subdomains. Preflight is not an authorization decision. XSS can bypass CSRF defenses by running in the trusted origin, so XSS prevention remains essential.

I would test forged forms, simple content types, allowed/unallowed origins, missing/invalid tokens, sibling subdomains and client-side URL manipulation.

title: Frontend Security Threat Modeling
description: Mapping assets, actors, entry points, trust boundaries and abuse cases before implementation.

blocks.title: Architect-level framing
blocks.content:
I would draw the system and data flows before selecting controls. Assets include the authenticated session, payment instructions, PII, approval authority, uploaded documents and audit evidence. Actors include legitimate users, malicious users, compromised accounts, attacker-controlled websites, a compromised third-party script and internal services. Trust boundaries exist at the browser, identity provider, BFF, APIs, object storage, notification channel and external vendors.

For every flow I would ask what can be spoofed, tampered with, disclosed, replayed or denied. Examples include login/redirect manipulation, CSRF payment submission, XSS through payee names or uploaded previews, IDOR by changing payment IDs, malicious files, WebSocket subscription to another user's events, analytics receiving PII, and a third-party script reading the page.

Then I would prioritize by business impact and feasibility. High-impact controls include server-side resource authorization, maker-checker separation, step-up authentication, transaction confirmation that displays authoritative server data, idempotency and replay protection, secure session architecture, strict content handling, file quarantine/scanning, scoped real-time subscriptions and complete audit records.

I would record assumptions—such as trusted corporate devices or same-site subdomains—because an assumption is a future vulnerability if it changes silently. Threats become security requirements and tests, with owners and residual risk accepted by the correct stakeholder. The model is revisited when a new integration or data flow appears.

The lead-level outcome is not a long generic threat list. It is a short set of concrete abuse cases connected to architecture, tests, telemetry and incident response.

title: Third-Party Script and Software Supply-Chain Security
description: Controlling npm dependencies, remote scripts, integrity, privileges, updates, SBOM and incident response.

blocks.title: Architect-level framing
blocks.content:
I would treat remote JavaScript as code executing with our application's origin privileges. Lockfiles and reproducible builds reduce unexpected change, while automated update PRs require tests and review rather than blind auto-merge. A software bill of materials and dependency inventory support incident response.

title: Secure File Upload and Download
description: Protecting file workflows against malicious content, path tricks, authorization errors, active previews and data leakage.

blocks.title: Architect-level framing
blocks.content:
I would assume every uploaded file, name, MIME type and extension is untrusted. The browser can provide early user feedback, but server-side controls are authoritative. The upload API enforces authentication, tenant/resource authorization, size limits, an allowlist of required file types, normalized generated storage names and content/magic-byte validation. Files are stored outside the web root or in isolated object storage.

New files enter quarantine. Malware scanning, document parsing and optional content-disarm processes happen before the file becomes available. Processing runs with minimal privileges and resource limits because parsers are attack surfaces. A successful HTTP upload response should not imply the document is approved; the UI shows scanning/processing state.

Preview is a separate risk. Active formats such as HTML or some document types should not be rendered in the application origin. Use safe transformed previews, forced download with a safe `Content-Disposition`, restrictive content type, a separate untrusted-content origin and sandboxing where appropriate. SVG and filename handling deserve explicit attention.

Download URLs are short-lived and scoped to the authorized object. The backend verifies the current user and resource on every request; an unpredictable ID is not authorization. Responses prevent caching when documents are sensitive and avoid exposing storage paths. Audit logs record who accessed which document without logging its content.

I would also protect availability: per-user quotas, rate limits, decompression-bomb limits, timeouts and cleanup of abandoned uploads. Tests include extension/MIME mismatch, polyglots, path names, oversized archives, cross-tenant IDs and expired links.

title: Secrets, Runtime Configuration and Environment Separation
description: Keeping secrets server-side while delivering safe public configuration and preventing environment mix-ups.

blocks.title: Architect-level framing
blocks.content:
I would state clearly that anything delivered to the browser is public. Angular environment files are build-time replacements, not secret storage. A user can inspect bundles, source maps, network requests and runtime objects. OAuth client secrets, private API keys, database credentials and signing keys must remain on trusted servers or secret-management systems.

I would classify configuration. Public frontend configuration includes API base URLs, non-secret client IDs, tenant-safe feature flags, telemetry endpoints and build metadata. It can be loaded at startup from a validated runtime configuration so one immutable frontend artifact can move through environments. Sensitive configuration stays in the BFF/backend and is never returned.

The runtime config endpoint/file should have a schema, safe defaults, version and cache strategy. It must not allow arbitrary script or endpoint injection; permitted origins and URL patterns should be constrained. The app should fail closed or enter a clear maintenance state when required config is invalid, not silently connect to a fallback production API.

Environment separation is enforced through deployment identity, DNS, certificates, CORS, OAuth redirect registration and backend authorization—not merely a colored header. CI should scan bundles and repositories for secrets, and source maps should follow a deliberate production policy. Build provenance and displayed build/version help incident diagnosis.

I would also avoid embedding business authorization in feature flags. Flags are public rollout inputs; APIs enforce capabilities independently. Rotation and revocation procedures must exist for any credential that was accidentally exposed.

Separate public UI configuration from server-side credentials.
Use one immutable artifact with validated runtime config where operationally useful.

title: Privacy, PII, Logging and Data Minimization
description: Designing browser storage, telemetry, analytics, masking, export and retention around sensitive user data.

blocks.title: Architect-level framing
blocks.content:
I would start from purpose and minimization. The frontend should receive only fields required for the current workflow, and highly sensitive identifiers should be masked or tokenized where full values are unnecessary. Hiding a value with CSS is not protection if the full value remains in the DOM or JavaScript object.

Logs, analytics and error reports should use an explicit allowlist schema. I would never send tokens, credentials, full identity numbers, account numbers, document content or arbitrary request bodies. User-entered text can contain PII, so capturing DOM snapshots, console logs and session replay needs separate privacy and security approval. Correlation IDs, route, build, operation code, duration and normalized error category are usually enough for diagnosis.

Client storage also needs classification. Avoid persisting sensitive data unless a clear offline requirement exists. If IndexedDB is required, define retention, logout/tenant-switch cleanup, schema migration, device threat assumptions and whether local encryption provides meaningful protection; keys accessible to the same compromised origin do not solve XSS.

The UI should prevent accidental disclosure through autocomplete, clipboard, downloads, browser cache and shared-device history where relevant. Screenshots and exports may require watermarking or audit depending on policy, but the backend remains the authority for access and download.

I would collaborate with legal/privacy/security to define lawful purpose and retention, but implementation should make the policy enforceable: typed telemetry events, redaction at source, server-side filtering as a second layer and automated tests that assert sensitive patterns never leave the browser.

title: State Management Strategy
description: Classifying local UI, URL, workflow and server state to avoid unnecessary global stores and duplicated truth.

blocks.title: Architect-level framing
blocks.content:
I would start by classifying state rather than debating libraries. Transient presentation state—whether a panel is open or which tab has focus—belongs close to the component. Shareable and restorable state such as search filters, sort and selected report date belongs in the URL. Cross-component feature workflow state can live in a feature-scoped store or service. Remote server state needs query, freshness, invalidation and error semantics, so I would manage it as server state rather than copy every response into a universal event store.

For each state item I would write down its owner, source of truth, lifetime, persistence, serialization and update authority. Derived values should be computed from canonical state instead of stored separately. For example, selected transaction details should derive from `selectedId` plus the entity cache, not be another mutable object that can drift.

Signals are well suited to synchronous local/derived UI state; RxJS remains valuable for asynchronous event streams, cancellation and composition. NgRx or another explicit event store is useful for complex shared workflows, auditability and strong conventions, but I would not require it for every form control or HTTP response.

I would migrate by selecting one confused feature, drawing its state graph, removing duplicates and adding a facade so components depend on intent and selectors rather than storage mechanics. Feature stores should be lazy-scoped when their lifetime is a route, and user-specific state must reset on logout or tenant change.

Success means a developer can answer 'where does this value come from, who can change it, and when is it stale?' without searching five services.

Define owner, source of truth, lifetime, persistence and update authority for every shared state.

title: Concurrent Requests and Race Conditions
description: Preventing stale reads, duplicate writes and out-of-order responses using cancellation, request identity and server concurrency.

blocks.title: Architect-level framing
blocks.content:
I would treat the read and write cases differently. Search is usually latest-intent-wins. The input stream should debounce noisy changes, ignore equivalent queries and cancel or disregard the previous request when a newer query arrives. In Angular/RxJS, `switchMap` expresses that policy. With fetch-style APIs, an `AbortController` or monotonically increasing request ID can provide the same behavior.

Cancellation is not enough for writes. The server may already have accepted a request even if the browser disconnects. For payment creation I would disable accidental repeated submission in the UI, but the authoritative protection is a server idempotency key tied to the logical operation. Retrying the same key returns the same outcome rather than creating another payment. For updates, version/ETag preconditions prevent lost updates when two users edit the same resource.

I would make concurrency semantics visible in the API contract. Which reads are latest-wins? Which writes are idempotent? Can operations be safely retried? What conflict status and payload are returned? The UI should distinguish timeout with unknown outcome from confirmed failure; for an unknown payment outcome it should query operation status before offering another submit.

In the client I would also prevent older route/component responses from mutating destroyed state and ensure loading indicators are keyed to the current request. Tests would deliberately reorder responses, delay acknowledgements, repeat clicks and simulate timeout after server commit.

The senior-level point is that RxJS operators control client observation, while correctness of side effects requires server-defined idempotency and concurrency.

Do not assume cancelled writes were not processed by the server.
Use server idempotency keys for retryable create operations.
Use ETag/version preconditions for conflicting updates.
Represent unknown outcome separately from confirmed failure.

title: Optimistic UI and Concurrency Control
description: Using optimistic updates safely with rollback, versioning, dependent caches and conflict UX.

blocks.title: Architect-level framing
blocks.content:
I would use optimistic UI only when the action is likely to succeed, reversible and understandable if it fails. Before the request, I capture the previous canonical state and apply a pending version with a visible sync indicator. The optimistic update should modify the same entity source used by every view, not only the current component.

The mutation carries the entity version or ETag. If the server accepts it, the response becomes the new canonical state and dependent queries are updated or invalidated. If validation or authorization fails, I roll back and show a specific message. If the version conflicts, I do not simply roll back and overwrite the user's work; I fetch the latest state and offer a merge/reapply experience appropriate to the field.

Multiple edits require sequencing. I can queue mutations per entity, collapse compatible changes or tag them with client mutation IDs so late responses do not overwrite newer optimistic state. A deleted or business-critical financial record may not be a good candidate for optimism at all.

The UI must distinguish local pending, confirmed, failed and conflicted states. Accessibility matters: status changes should be announced without stealing focus. Offline optimism becomes an outbox/synchronization design, not just a temporary in-memory patch.

I would test slow responses, rejection, conflict, reordered acknowledgements, navigation away and refresh. Telemetry should measure rollback/conflict frequency; frequent rollback indicates the product is hiding too much uncertainty and should use pessimistic confirmation.

title: Complex Forms, Drafts and Autosave
description: Architecting large workflows with validation layers, draft persistence, versioning, partial save and safe navigation.

blocks.title: Architect-level framing
blocks.content:
I would model the workflow as a domain process, not one enormous form component. Each section owns a typed sub-form and maps to a draft command/view model. A coordinator manages step status, navigation, server draft version and final submission. Conditional rules should be expressed in testable domain/form logic rather than scattered template conditions.

Validation has layers. Synchronous client validation gives immediate feedback; asynchronous checks such as account eligibility are debounced/cancelled and treated as advisory until the server validates the complete command. The backend remains authoritative and returns structured field/global errors. Hidden fields must not silently retain values that should be cleared by a business rule.

Autosave should be incremental and explicit. I would debounce meaningful changes, save only valid/serializable draft data or allow incomplete drafts under a separate contract, and attach a draft version/ETag. The UI shows saving, saved, offline and conflict states. On another device or stale tab, a version conflict prompts reload/merge rather than last-write-wins data loss.

For resilience, local storage may hold a short-lived recovery copy only if data sensitivity permits; cross-device continuation requires a server draft. Attachments use independent resumable upload sessions linked to the draft. Final submission is a separate idempotent command that validates all sections, locks or versions the draft and returns an operation/result.

I would guard navigation with unsaved changes carefully, preserve accessibility and focus on validation summaries, and test conditional paths rather than only the happy sequence. Telemetry should reveal save latency, conflicts, abandoned steps and validation hotspots without logging form values.

title: Search and Typeahead at Scale
description: Designing debounced, cancellable, accessible search with ranking, caching, privacy and server limits.

blocks.title: Architect-level framing
blocks.content:
I would define the search contract first: minimum query length, supported filters, result groups, ranking, page/cursor, maximum results and latency target. The browser should not fan out uncontrolled requests to every service. A search API or BFF can own federation, security trimming, ranking and response limits.

The input stream debounces text, normalizes whitespace, ignores equivalent queries and uses latest-query-wins cancellation. The UI distinguishes initial, loading, empty, partial and error states. Short/broad queries can show recent items or require more characters rather than performing expensive unbounded search. Results return stable IDs, safe highlighted fragments or match metadata; the frontend should not render raw HTML from the search index.

Caching should be small and privacy-aware. Recent exact queries can be cached briefly, but user/tenant boundaries and sensitive terms prevent a global persistent cache. Prefetching is rarely justified until selection probability is known.

Accessibility is part of the component contract. Use an established combobox pattern with keyboard navigation, active-descendant or managed focus, status announcements and a clear relationship between input and listbox. Do not move focus unexpectedly while results update.

On the backend, use indexed search, timeouts, rate limits and authorization before ranking. Partial source failure can be represented per group. I would measure keystroke-to-results p95, cancellation rate, backend query cost, zero-result rate and selection success, and use those signals to tune debounce and ranking.

title: Real-Time Updates, Reconnects and Backpressure
description: Choosing polling, SSE or WebSockets and maintaining ordered, idempotent state under disconnects and event bursts.

blocks.title: Architect-level framing
blocks.content:
I would choose the transport from communication needs. If updates are mainly server-to-client and standard HTTP infrastructure matters, Server-Sent Events may be sufficient. WebSockets fit bidirectional low-latency interaction. Polling remains reasonable for low-frequency data. The transport choice does not solve consistency.

The client should load a versioned snapshot, then subscribe from a cursor/sequence. Every event carries an event ID, entity ID and version so updates are idempotent and stale/out-of-order events can be rejected. On reconnect, the client resumes after the last confirmed cursor or reloads a snapshot when the retention gap is too large. Exponential backoff with jitter avoids reconnect storms.

At high volume, I would not render every event. The ingestion layer updates a normalized in-memory model, coalesces multiple updates for the same entity and publishes to the UI at a bounded frame/time cadence. Low-priority data can be sampled or aggregated. The standard `WebSocket` API has no built-in backpressure, so queue length and processing rate must be controlled; in some cases server-side throttling, topic filtering or a stream-capable approach is required.

Subscriptions are authorized by user, tenant and topic. Tokens are renewed or the connection is re-established safely, and logs never contain payload secrets. A single managed connection per application/session avoids a connection per widget.

I would measure event lag, dropped/coalesced count, queue depth, reconnects, snapshot recovery, CPU, memory and UI INP. Correctness under disconnect is more important than a demo that works on a stable local network.

title: Multi-Tab Synchronization
description: Coordinating logout, account switching, drafts, cache invalidation and singleton work across browser tabs.

blocks.title: Architect-level framing
blocks.content:
I would classify what must be synchronized. Logout and account/tenant switching are security events and should propagate immediately. Cache invalidation and feature flags may propagate eventually. Editing the same draft needs conflict detection rather than blindly copying form values between tabs.

A `BroadcastChannel` is a useful same-origin mechanism for small coordination messages such as `SESSION_LOGOUT`, `TENANT_CHANGED` or `ENTITY_INVALIDATED`. A storage event can be a fallback where needed. Messages contain a version, source tab ID and minimal non-sensitive payload; they are hints, not trusted authorization. On receiving logout, each tab clears user state, stops streams/workers and navigates to a safe signed-out screen.

For drafts, I would use server or IndexedDB versions and a lease/last-editor indication. If two tabs edit concurrently, both save with `If-Match`; one receives a conflict and must merge/reload. Electing a leader tab can prevent duplicate polling or WebSocket connections, but leader election must handle tab crashes and visibility changes. Often a shared worker or server connection strategy is more complex than the saved resources justify, so I would measure first.

I would avoid storing sensitive session material in channel messages or localStorage. Account switching should partition caches by session/tenant and discard old data before the new context renders. Browser tabs may be suspended, so each tab also validates session/config on focus or API response rather than relying only on real-time messages.

Tests cover missed messages, sleeping tabs, simultaneous logout/login, stale draft save and channel unavailability.

title: Normalized Data and Cross-View Consistency
description: Using entity identity, query membership and derived selectors to keep multiple views consistent without one massive store.

blocks.title: Architect-level framing
blocks.content:
I would separate entity data from query results. A normalized cache stores each customer once by stable ID, while queries store ordered IDs, pagination metadata, filters and freshness. Components resolve IDs through the entity source, so when the canonical customer changes, every view that references that ID sees the new name or status.

Normalization is useful when the same entities appear in many views and mutations are frequent. It is not mandatory for every response; one-off report rows with no identity can remain query-local. The mapping layer must preserve API ownership and avoid turning every backend payload into one universal client model.

A mutation response should return the canonical entity plus version. The client updates that entity and decides whether query membership or aggregates changed. Changing a display name normally preserves list membership; changing region may invalidate region-filtered queries; deleting an entity removes it from relevant query IDs. Derived counts should not be stored separately unless they have an authoritative server source or a clear invalidation rule.

I would expose selectors/facades rather than let components directly mutate maps. Cache entries are partitioned by tenant/user and evicted by policy. For cross-user updates, normal freshness or event mechanisms still apply—normalization only prevents duplicate local copies.

Testing focuses on mutation propagation across views, query membership changes, deletion, partial entities and version ordering. The goal is coherent local representation, not forcing all application state into a single global store.

title: Background Jobs, Progress and Notifications
description: Designing long-running exports, imports and calculations with idempotent submission, durable status and recovery.

blocks.title: Architect-level framing
blocks.content:
I would model report generation as a durable server job. The browser submits the report definition with an idempotency key, and the server quickly returns `202 Accepted` with a job ID and status URL. The job record contains owner, tenant, parameters, state, progress, timestamps, result metadata and failure code. Processing is decoupled from the browser connection.

The UI stores the job ID in route or server-side recent-jobs state, so refresh and another device can recover it. Progress can be polled with backoff, delivered by SSE/WebSocket, or combined—real-time for responsiveness with polling/status fetch as the recovery source. The status endpoint is authoritative and fully authorized; guessing a job ID must not expose another user's result.

State transitions are explicit: queued, running, succeeded, failed, cancelled and expired. Progress should be honest; when exact percentage is impossible, show stage/activity rather than a fake linear bar. Cancellation is best-effort and must distinguish 'cancel requested' from 'cancelled'. Result downloads use a short-lived authorized URL, retention policy and audit.

A repeated submission with the same idempotency key should return the existing job. Jobs may outlive frontend deployments, so status/result contracts must be backward compatible. Notifications can alert the user when complete without making push delivery the only recovery mechanism.

I would test worker retry, duplicate messages, refresh, logout/login, cancellation race, expired results and mixed frontend versions.

title: Backend for Frontend (BFF)
description: Using a frontend-owned server boundary for token isolation, aggregation, view models and resilient downstream orchestration.

blocks.title: Architect-level framing
blocks.content:
I would introduce a BFF when it creates concrete value: keeping OAuth tokens server-side, reducing browser chattiness, hiding unstable service topology, producing frontend-specific view models or centralizing web-session concerns. I would not add one as a pass-through proxy for every request.

The browser authenticates through the BFF and receives an opaque Secure HttpOnly session cookie. The BFF owns OAuth token handling, CSRF protection, correlation and policy needed for the web channel. It calls downstream services with least-privileged credentials and returns contracts designed for the UI. Aggregation should run independent calls in parallel with timeouts and explicitly represent optional partial failures.

The boundary is important: the BFF may compose and reshape data, but authoritative domain rules remain in domain services. Otherwise the organization creates a second business backend that is difficult to reuse and test. I would organize BFF endpoints by frontend capability, use generated/validated downstream clients, set request budgets and prevent uncontrolled N+1 fan-out.

Resilience includes per-dependency timeout, bounded retries only for safe operations, circuit/bulkhead strategy where justified, request cancellation propagation and cache rules. Observability must connect browser journey -> BFF -> downstream traces without logging sensitive payloads. Scaling and deployment follow the frontend's availability needs, but API compatibility must support older browser builds during rollout.

I would measure whether the BFF reduces end-to-end p95, token exposure and client complexity. If it simply adds latency and another team handoff, the design is wrong.

title: Micro-Frontend Architecture
description: Evaluating independent deployment, runtime composition, contracts, shared dependencies, identity, design system and failure isolation.

blocks.title: Architect-level framing
blocks.content:
I would first verify the organizational requirement. Micro-frontends solve independent ownership and deployment constraints; they are not required to achieve code modularity. If one release train and one team already work well, a modular monolith is cheaper.

When the need is real, I would align frontends to stable business domains, not individual pages or widgets. A shell owns top-level navigation, identity/session integration, route composition, common telemetry and a small design-system contract. Each domain owns its route subtree, tests, deployment and production support. Cross-frontend communication should be minimal: URL/navigation, versioned events for rare coordination or backend workflows. A shared global mutable store would recreate a distributed monolith.

Runtime integration requires explicit policies: supported Angular/runtime versions, singleton sharing, dependency duplication, remote loading timeout, CSP, fallback UI, compatibility and rollback. Sharing every dependency tightly couples release versions; sharing nothing inflates bytes. I would share a deliberately small stable platform layer and permit domain libraries to evolve independently.

Design-system versioning and visual governance prevent the product from feeling fragmented. Authentication is centralized enough to provide one session, but each backend still authorizes. Observability tags every remote and build so failures can be isolated.

I would begin with one low-coupling domain and prove independent deploy/rollback, performance and incident ownership. If the first adoption needs coordinated releases for every change, the architecture has failed its purpose.

title: Design System at Scale
description: Building accessible tokens, components, patterns, documentation, governance, versioning and contribution workflows.

blocks.title: Architect-level framing
blocks.content:
I would define the design system as a product, not a component dump. Its layers include design tokens, accessible primitives, composed components, interaction/content patterns, documentation, test tooling, release/version policy and contribution governance. Product designers and engineers jointly own the contract.

I would begin with high-frequency/high-risk primitives: typography, spacing, color, focus, buttons, inputs, form errors, dialogs, menus and tables. Native semantic HTML is the default; ARIA fills gaps rather than replacing semantics. Keyboard, focus restoration, screen-reader names, motion preferences, RTL and responsive states are part of the component API and acceptance tests.

Tokens should express semantic intent—surface, critical text, focus indicator—not raw product-specific color names. Theming can map tenant/brand values to these tokens while preserving contrast and interaction states. Components expose deliberate slots and inputs rather than arbitrary CSS overrides that break internals.

Adoption requires excellent documentation, examples, generators, design assets, migration guides and fast support. I would version packages semantically, publish deprecations and codemods where possible, and keep release notes linked to visual/accessibility changes. Contributions follow a lightweight RFC/review process and include design, tests and ownership.

Automated unit, visual regression and accessibility checks run for components, but manual keyboard and assistive-technology testing remains necessary for complex patterns. I would measure product adoption, duplicated components, upgrade lag, accessibility defects and time to deliver common UI—not only npm downloads.

title: CSR, SSR, Prerendering and Hydration Strategy
description: Choosing rendering per route based on SEO, first content, personalization, server cost, caching and interaction needs.

blocks.title: Architect-level framing
blocks.content:
I would choose rendering per route rather than apply SSR uniformly. Public marketing and documentation routes benefit from crawlable HTML, fast first content and CDN caching; prerendering may be ideal when content changes through deployment. Personalized public content or frequently changing pages may justify SSR. The authenticated analytics dashboard often gains less from SEO and may be simpler as CSR, unless measured first-render requirements justify server rendering.

SSR changes the architecture. Browser-only APIs need guards, server requests need authentication and timeouts, HTML must avoid leaking user data into shared caches, and server/client rendering must be deterministic enough for hydration. Hydration reuses server-rendered DOM rather than destroying and recreating it, improving visual stability, but direct DOM manipulation or invalid HTML can cause mismatches.

I would use route-level data transfer carefully to avoid the browser immediately repeating server requests, and I would ensure personalized responses are private and correctly varied. Heavy below-the-fold areas can use Angular deferrable views; incremental hydration can delay code and activation for selected regions while preserving server-rendered content.

The decision includes operational cost: rendering capacity, edge/cache strategy, monitoring, deployment and failure fallback. If SSR fails, the system should have a deliberate behavior rather than a blank page. I would compare TTFB, LCP, INP, server cost and cache hit ratio for each route type.

The answer is not 'SSR is faster'. SSR can improve initial content while increasing server time and hydration work; measure the whole user journey.

blocks.title: Architect-level framing

I would define the flag's purpose and lifecycle before implementation. This is a release flag, not a permanent permission rule. It needs an owner, creation date, expected removal date, safe default and rollback behavior. The decision should be evaluated consistently—preferably server/BFF-side when it affects API behavior or security—and returned as a stable assignment so the user does not switch experiences mid-transaction.

The frontend receives only public variation information. It should not use a flag to authorize an operation; the backend enforces capabilities independently. Targeting can use employee group, tenant allowlist or deterministic percentage bucketing based on a stable pseudonymous key. Random evaluation on every page load creates inconsistent cohorts and corrupts experiment data.

title: Frontend Deployment, Versioning and Rollback
description: Immutable releases, atomic publication, old-tab compatibility, canaries, telemetry and rapid recovery.

blocks.title: Architect-level framing
blocks.content:
I would make frontend releases immutable and assume old clients remain active. Build assets use content hashes, and deployment publishes a complete new set atomically. The app shell points to the new hashes, but previous assets remain available for a grace period so old tabs can lazy-load their original chunks. Deleting old assets immediately is a common cause of chunk-load failures.

The backend must maintain compatibility across the frontend rollout window. I would use expand-and-contract API changes: add the new field/behavior, deploy compatible clients, observe adoption, then remove the old contract only after old builds are no longer supported. Rollback is impossible if the backend has already made a one-way incompatible change.

I would release through canary or staged traffic where infrastructure allows, with telemetry segmented by frontend build. Health gates include JavaScript error rate, chunk failures, authentication, API errors, Core Web Vitals and critical journey success. A build/version endpoint and visible support metadata make incidents diagnosable.

The application should detect a chunk/version mismatch and offer a controlled refresh, preserving unsaved work where possible. Service-worker update behavior must be coordinated so the UI, chunks and IndexedDB schema are not mixed incompatibly. Database/client data migrations should be backward compatible and reversible during the window.

Rollback means repointing the app shell/manifest to a known immutable release, not rebuilding under pressure. I would rehearse it and retain provenance, source maps and dependency records for every release.
