title: Monorepo and Shared Library Governance
description: Structuring packages, ownership, release/version strategy, dependency constraints and avoiding a shared-library monolith.

blocks.title: Architect-level framing
blocks.content:
I would first separate repository topology from runtime architecture. A monorepo can improve atomic changes, refactoring and consistent tooling, but it does not require every application to depend on every library or deploy together.

I would define package categories and ownership: design-system primitives, platform/identity/telemetry, domain libraries and application features. Each library has a clear public entry point, dependency tags and no deep imports. Domain libraries should not become a way for applications to share mutable business state; stable contracts and APIs are safer.

Build tooling should use an accurate project graph, incremental computation and affected-only tests/builds. Caching can be local/remote when outputs are deterministic and secrets are excluded. A change to a leaf feature should not rebuild unrelated applications; a change to a central design token may legitimately affect many.

Versioning depends on deployment model. Internal source libraries in one coordinated repository can use lockstep source compatibility, while independently published packages need semantic versioning, deprecation and consumer migration. I would avoid publishing dozens of packages solely for architecture appearance.

Governance includes code owners, API review for widely consumed libraries, dependency budgets and a promotion rule: code becomes shared only after a stable reuse pattern and owner exist. Duplicate a small utility rather than create a central package that nobody owns. Large 'utils' and 'common' packages are split by responsibility or removed.

I would measure affected project count, cache hit rate, CI duration, shared-package change frequency, upgrade lag and cross-team review dependencies.

title: Error Handling and Resilience
description: Designing localized failure, retry policy, graceful degradation, correlation and recovery instead of global generic errors.

blocks.title: Architect-level framing
blocks.content:
I would classify errors by scope and recoverability before deciding how to display them. A failure in an optional widget should not blank the whole dashboard. The page can render successful capabilities, show a localized error for the failed widget and provide retry only when the operation is safe. A failure in identity or required account context may make the whole route invalid and should use a route-level recovery state.

The HTTP layer can normalize transport and server problem details into stable error categories, but it should not convert every error into a toast. The feature owns the user message and recovery action because it knows the business context. Validation errors map to fields or a summary, authorization errors refresh permission/context, authentication expiry follows a controlled reauthentication flow, and transient reads may retry with bounded backoff and jitter.

Writes need more caution. A timeout does not prove the server failed. For a payment, the UI should use an idempotency key/operation ID and query status before allowing another submission. Automatic retries are limited to operations whose API contract declares them safe. Circuit or bulkhead behavior normally lives at the BFF/service layer, though the frontend can stop aggressive retries and degrade gracefully.

Every user-visible failure should carry a safe correlation or support reference when useful. Telemetry records route, build, operation and normalized category, not sensitive payloads. Empty data is not the same as error; stale fallback data must be labelled with age and only used when acceptable.

I would test partial failure, retries, offline transitions, expired session, unknown write outcome and recovery after service restoration. The goal is to preserve safe useful work without hiding correctness uncertainty.

title: Observability and Real User Monitoring
description: Connecting user journeys, browser errors, web vitals, API traces and release versions while controlling privacy and telemetry cost.

blocks.title: Architect-level framing
blocks.content:
I would instrument from the user's perspective. Infrastructure uptime can be green while the browser fails to load a chunk, spends two seconds on the main thread or receives a successful response it cannot render. I would collect JavaScript errors, unhandled promise rejections, chunk/resource failures, API latency/error categories, Core Web Vitals and a small set of business journey timings such as login, account search and payment completion.

Every event includes build/version, route, browser/device class, region, anonymous session or trace context and correlation ID where available. It must exclude tokens, full URLs with sensitive query values, request bodies and PII. High-cardinality fields such as raw user IDs should not become metric labels; sampling and aggregation control volume and cost.

Distributed tracing can connect browser document load or API request to BFF/downstream services using W3C trace context, subject to CORS and security policy. I would be cautious because browser OpenTelemetry instrumentation remains less mature than server instrumentation; the design should use stable internal event schemas and not depend on one vendor.

Dashboards compare builds and user segments. Alerts focus on user-impact signals: elevated payment failure, p75 INP/LCP regression, chunk failures or login completion—not every console error. Source maps are stored securely and associated with immutable builds so stack traces are actionable.

I would add release annotations and canary health gates, then use session-level breadcrumbs for diagnosis without capturing sensitive DOM. The observability system should answer: which users/builds are affected, where time was spent, which dependency failed and whether the last release changed it.

title: Accessibility and Internationalization at Scale
description: Embedding semantic interaction, WCAG, focus, RTL, pluralization, locale formatting and translation workflows into architecture.

blocks.title: Architect-level framing
blocks.content:
I would make accessibility and internationalization platform constraints rather than final QA activities. The design system provides semantic primitives with keyboard behavior, visible focus, focus restoration, accessible names, error association, reduced-motion support and tested responsive states. Product teams compose these primitives instead of rebuilding dialogs, menus and grids.

Native HTML is the starting point. ARIA is used only where native semantics cannot express the pattern, following established interaction guidance. Automated checks run in component and end-to-end tests, but they cannot prove usability; critical journeys receive manual keyboard, zoom/high-contrast and screen-reader testing. Sticky headers, dialogs and virtualized grids are tested for focus not being hidden or trapped.

For localization, content uses stable message IDs and full sentences rather than concatenated fragments. The translation system supports plural/select rules, date/number/currency formats and locale-specific calendars where required. CSS uses logical properties so RTL does not require a second stylesheet. Layouts tolerate text expansion, and icons with directional meaning are mirrored deliberately while neutral icons are not.

Locale and language are separate from authorization and tenant. Server values carry machine formats; display formatting occurs at the UI boundary. User-entered data is not automatically translated. The application handles missing translations safely and avoids embedding HTML in translation strings unless a controlled rich-message system exists.

Governance includes accessibility/i18n acceptance criteria, reviewer training, design annotations, translation preview environments and defect ownership. I would measure automated violations, manual critical-flow results, untranslated strings, layout overflow and real assistive-technology feedback.

title: Frontend Testing Strategy for Enterprise Systems
description: Balancing unit, component, contract, integration, end-to-end, visual, accessibility, performance and production tests.

blocks.title: Architect-level framing
blocks.content:
I would align tests to risk and contracts, not maximize one test count. Pure domain transformations and reducers deserve fast unit tests. Components should be tested through rendered behavior—what the user can see and do—rather than private methods and implementation details. Feature integration tests cover forms, state, routing and mocked network boundaries.

API mismatch is addressed with schema and consumer/producer contract tests, not only frontend mocks that always return the expected shape. A smaller set of end-to-end tests exercises critical journeys against realistic environments: login, role-based access, payment creation, failure recovery and download. These tests should be deterministic, own their data and avoid duplicating every validation branch already covered below.

The design system gets visual regression and accessibility tests because one defect affects many products. Performance budgets and targeted browser/device tests protect high-risk routes. Security checks include dependency scanning, dangerous-sink rules and authorization tests at the API level; a frontend E2E test cannot prove backend authorization alone.

I would remove brittle tests that assert component internals or snapshots with no business meaning. Test helpers expose user actions and stable roles/labels. Network mocks should simulate delay, reordering, partial failure and malformed responses. Flaky tests are treated as defects with owners and quarantine limits, not endlessly rerun.

Release confidence also uses production observability, canaries and rollback. No pre-production suite covers every browser/network combination. I would track escaped defects, suite duration, flaky rate and which test layer caught issues, then invest where risk remains.

blocks.question: Your suite has 8,000 brittle unit tests but production defects still occur in API integration, permissions and browser behavior. How would you redesign testing?
blocks.answer:
I would align tests to risk and contracts, not maximize one test count. Pure domain transformations and reducers deserve fast unit tests. Components should be tested through rendered behavior—what the user can see and do—rather than private methods and implementation details. Feature integration tests cover forms, state, routing and mocked network boundaries.

API mismatch is addressed with schema and consumer/producer contract tests, not only frontend mocks that always return the expected shape. A smaller set of end-to-end tests exercises critical journeys against realistic environments: login, role-based access, payment creation, failure recovery and download. These tests should be deterministic, own their data and avoid duplicating every validation branch already covered below.

The design system gets visual regression and accessibility tests because one defect affects many products. Performance budgets and targeted browser/device tests protect high-risk routes. Security checks include dependency scanning, dangerous-sink rules and authorization tests at the API level; a frontend E2E test cannot prove backend authorization alone.

I would remove brittle tests that assert component internals or snapshots with no business meaning. Test helpers expose user actions and stable roles/labels. Network mocks should simulate delay, reordering, partial failure and malformed responses. Flaky tests are treated as defects with owners and quarantine limits, not endlessly rerun.

Release confidence also uses production observability, canaries and rollback. No pre-production suite covers every browser/network combination. I would track escaped defects, suite duration, flaky rate and which test layer caught issues, then invest where risk remains.

blocks.question: How many end-to-end tests should a project have?
blocks.answer: There is no fixed number. Enough to protect high-value cross-system journeys and deployment confidence, but not every branch. I would use risk, runtime and defect history to decide.

title: Browser Compatibility and Progressive Enhancement
description: Designing capability detection, supported-browser policy, polyfills, graceful fallback and enterprise webview testing.

blocks.title: Architect-level framing
blocks.content:
I would begin with an explicit supported-browser matrix based on users, contracts and security support—not 'all browsers'. Analytics can inform usage, but legal, accessibility and managed-device requirements may add browsers with small percentages. Unsupported versions should receive a clear policy rather than unpredictable failure.

I would distinguish syntax/transpilation, API availability and behavior differences. The build target handles supported JavaScript syntax; polyfills can provide some standard APIs; CSS and Web APIs need feature detection and fallback. User-agent sniffing is a last resort for known platform bugs, not the main architecture.

Progressive enhancement means the core task remains usable with broadly supported capabilities, while richer features activate when available. A large local export may use File System Access where supported and fall back to a server-generated download elsewhere. Background sync, notifications and advanced media APIs should be optional enhancements. Security-sensitive features should fail closed, not silently use an unsafe fallback.

I would encapsulate browser-specific capability behind adapters so product components do not contain repeated platform branches. Automated tests cover the supported matrix for critical journeys, and real-device/webview testing targets high-risk integrations. Compatibility telemetry records safe capability/browser information with build and failure category.

Dropping a browser is a product/security decision with notice, migration guidance and evidence. Conversely, shipping large polyfills to every user for one legacy client may be worse than a separate degraded path.

The senior answer balances reach, security, bundle cost and maintenance while preserving a reliable core workflow.
keyPoints: Define and publish a supported-browser/security policy from real requirements.
Separate build syntax support, polyfills and runtime capability detection.
Use progressive enhancement for optional advanced APIs.
Encapsulate platform differences behind capability adapters.
Fail safely for security-critical unsupported behavior.
Test critical journeys on the supported matrix and use field telemetry.

blocks.question: When is user-agent detection acceptable?
blocks.answer: For narrowly scoped, documented workarounds to known browser bugs when feature detection cannot distinguish the behavior. It should have tests, an owner and a removal condition.
